name: Zircon Grey
lede: Zircon Grey is a warm, reddish grey first plated by Ridgway in 1912, a color that keeps turning up on the same canvases as [[dark-silver-pink]].

sections.title: A warm grey, named for a mineral
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 atlas plates this grey, and the 1955 ISCC-NBS circular later classed it as reddish gray, 6.1 units from its own block center[1]. The Munsell notation is a neutral N 4.9, meaning the system records almost no hue at all for it, just a value step [1]. Our sources tag the name as a mineral word, zircon, but do not document who coined the color name or when [1].

The closest named color on screen is [[rose-castor]], 3.2 units away and described as almost the same; [[dark-heliotrope-grey]] and [[fontainebleau]] sit at the same distance [3]. More tellingly, our archive finds Zircon Grey sharing canvases with Dark Silver Pink far more than chance would predict, a lift of 12.6[3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this grey in 1.13 percent of 23,781 paintings, 269 of them, and the within-painting lens isolates it as a dominant area in 138, as photographed [2]. That ranks it ahead of 64 percent of the named colors we track [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 41 of 1,674 paintings, present in 2.4 percent of the 1,674 paintings (41 of them) dated to that century, 2.9 times its museums' baseline rate [2].

Inside a painting it most often plays a mid-tone, 33 percent of its 138 appearances by lightness rank [2]. The earliest match in our archive is a painting dated to 1279, 633 years before Ridgway's 1912 record of the name; that gap marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not the pigment itself, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. It is also over-represented in French painting, 2.1 times the expected rate, 40 of 3,443 French works [2].

origin.source: Ridgway, Color Standards and Color Nomenclature
